title: The Cerrado: Two Sides of Farming

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *en cambio*, *por el contrario*, *al contrario*, *no obstante* and *ahora bien* from B2 Unit 30. Each sets one idea against another in its own way. The Cerrado, a savanna that became a farming giant, has a productive side and an environmental side. Here the markers work on the Cerrado.

sections.title: Contrast markers in the Cerrado
rows: Durante siglos se consideró un suelo pobre; en cambio, hoy produce mucha soja.
*en cambio*: a comparison, then and now
La agricultura no destruyó el Cerrado de golpe; por el contrario, avanzó poco a poco.
*por el contrario*: the opposite of what was said
La soja trajo ingresos; no obstante, se perdió gran parte de la vegetación nativa.
*no obstante*: a fact that does not cancel the first
El Cerrado produce mucha soja. Ahora bien, de allí nacen también grandes ríos.
*ahora bien*: adds a point that limits what you accepted

items.spanish: Los productores defienden la agricultura; los ambientalistas, en cambio, piden proteger lo que queda.
items.english: Producers defend farming; environmentalists, on the other hand, ask to protect what is left.

items.spanish: El Cerrado no es una región vacía; al contrario, tiene muchas especies.
items.english: The Cerrado is not an empty region; on the contrary, it has many species.

items.spanish: La región exporta mucho; no obstante, el agua es un tema de debate.
items.english: The region exports a lot; nevertheless, water is a subject of debate.

sections.content: *Pero* is the everyday word. These markers usually start a new clause, after a full stop or a semicolon, with a comma after them. Choose by the kind of contrast: a comparison (*en cambio*), the opposite (*por el contrario*, *al contrario*), a fact that does not stop you (*no obstante*) or a limit (*ahora bien*).
